title: Leather Selection Guide
body_html:
Leather Selection Guide

Overview

Leather is a popular material for laser cutting and engraving due to its unique texture, durability, and natural appearance. It is widely used in custom accessories, wallets, handbags, shoes, labels, patches, ornaments, and personalized products.

However, leather is not a single material category. Different types of leather vary significantly in composition, thickness, surface treatment, and processing behavior. Natural leather, synthetic leather, and coated leather may produce completely different laser results.

Choosing the correct leather before processing is essential for achieving clean cuts, high-quality engraving, and safe operation.

This guide explains the different types of leather and provides recommendations for selecting suitable materials for laser cutting and engraving.

 

Understanding Leather

Leather is a flexible material produced by treating animal hides through processes such as tanning, drying, and finishing.

Unlike engineered materials such as MDF or acrylic, leather has natural variations in:

  • Fiber structure
  • Thickness
  • Surface texture
  • Moisture content
  • Oil and dye content

These characteristics affect laser absorption, cutting speed, engraving contrast, and edge appearance.

When exposed to laser energy:

  1. The laser heats and removes the leather fibers.
  2. Organic materials decompose and vaporize.
  3. The cut edge becomes darker due to carbonization.
  4. Engraved areas develop contrast through surface modification.

Because leather is a natural material, small variations between sheets are normal.

 

Genuine Leather vs Synthetic Leather

The first step in selecting leather is understanding whether the material is natural or synthetic.

Genuine Leather

Genuine leather is made from animal hide and retains a natural fiber structure.

Common types include:

  • Cowhide
  • Sheepskin
  • Goatskin
  • Pigskin

Advantages for laser processing:

  • Natural texture
  • Premium appearance
  • Good engraving contrast
  • Suitable for custom products

Typical applications:

  • Wallets
  • Bags
  • Shoes
  • Belts
  • Accessories
  • Luxury goods

The appearance after engraving depends heavily on the tanning method and surface finish.

Synthetic Leather

Synthetic leather is manufactured using polymer coatings applied to fabric or synthetic substrates.

Common types include:

  • PU leather
  • PVC leather
  • Microfiber leather

Advantages include:

  • Consistent thickness
  • Lower cost
  • Wide range of colors
  • Uniform appearance

However, laser compatibility depends on the chemical composition of the coating.

 

Understanding Different Leather Types

Full-Grain Leather

Full-grain leather uses the outermost layer of the hide with minimal surface modification.

Characteristics:

  • Natural grain pattern
  • High durability
  • Premium appearance
  • Unique surface variations

Laser processing results:

  • Strong engraving contrast
  • Natural texture enhancement
  • Slight variation between pieces

Typical applications:

  • Premium wallets
  • High-end accessories
  • Luxury goods

Top-Grain Leather

Top-grain leather has the surface lightly corrected to remove imperfections.

Characteristics:

  • More uniform appearance
  • Smooth surface
  • Consistent processing results

Laser engraving usually produces predictable patterns and clean contrast.

Common applications:

  • Bags
  • Fashion accessories
  • Commercial products

Suede and Nubuck Leather

Suede and nubuck have a soft, textured surface created by processing the inner or outer fibers of the hide.

Characteristics:

  • Soft texture
  • Matte appearance
  • High absorbency

Laser processing considerations:

  • Engraving contrast may be subtle.
  • Excessive heat can damage the surface texture.
  • Lower power settings are often preferred.

 

PU Leather

Polyurethane (PU) leather is one of the most commonly used synthetic leathers.

Characteristics:

  • Flexible
  • Lightweight
  • Available in many colors
  • Uniform thickness

PU leather may be suitable for laser processing if the coating composition is confirmed.

Potential applications:

  • Fashion accessories
  • Decorative products
  • Labels
  • Small crafts

Always verify the manufacturer's material specifications before processing.

 

PVC Leather

Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) leather is a synthetic leather containing PVC coatings.

PVC leather is generally not recommended for laser processing.

During laser cutting, PVC may release:

  • Hydrogen chloride gas
  • Corrosive fumes
  • Harmful decomposition products

These gases may:

  • Damage machine components
  • Corrode optical systems
  • Create unsafe working conditions

Warning

Never laser process PVC leather unless the material has been specifically verified as laser-safe by the manufacturer.

 

Choosing the Right Leather Thickness

Leather thickness is usually measured in millimeters or ounces.

The appropriate thickness depends on the application.

Thicker leather generally requires:

  • Higher laser power
  • Slower cutting speeds
  • More effective exhaust
  • Proper focus adjustment

 

Surface Treatments

Leather may receive different surface finishes that affect laser results.

Natural Finish

Natural leather with minimal coating usually provides:

  • Strong engraving contrast
  • Natural texture
  • Variable appearance

Painted or Dyed Leather

Color-treated leather is widely used for decorative products.

Laser engraving can remove or modify the surface color, creating contrast.

Results depend on:

  • Dye type
  • Coating thickness
  • Surface finish

Coated Leather

Some leather products include protective coatings.

These coatings may:

  • Melt during processing
  • Produce additional smoke
  • Affect engraving quality

Always test coated leather before production.

 

Choosing Leather for Laser Engraving

For engraving applications, consider:

Light-Colored Leather

Usually provides:

  • Strong contrast after engraving
  • Clear patterns
  • Better visibility

Dark-Colored Leather

May produce less visible engraving because the surface color is already dark.

However, some finishes can create attractive tonal effects.

Vegetable-Tanned Leather

Vegetable-tanned leather is widely used for laser engraving because:

  • It has a natural surface
  • Engraving creates strong contrast
  • It develops a unique appearance over time

It is commonly used for:

  • Wallets
  • Covers
  • Handmade leather goods

 

Storage Recommendations

Proper storage helps maintain leather quality before processing.

Recommended practices:

  • Store leather in a dry environment.
  • Keep material flat to prevent deformation.
  • Avoid direct sunlight.
  • Protect surfaces from scratches.
  • Prevent excessive humidity exposure.

Leather that absorbs moisture may produce inconsistent cutting and engraving results.

 

Materials to Avoid

Do not process leather products with unknown compositions.

Avoid materials containing:

  • PVC coatings
  • Unknown plastic films
  • Metallic coatings without verification
  • Chemical treatments unsuitable for laser processing

If the material composition is unknown, consult the supplier before laser processing.

 

Summary

Leather is a versatile material for laser cutting and engraving, but successful processing depends heavily on material selection. Genuine leather, PU leather, and specialty leather products can produce excellent results when their composition is suitable for laser processing.

When selecting leather, consider the leather type, thickness, surface treatment, and chemical composition. Vegetable-tanned leather and high-quality genuine leather are often preferred for engraving, while PVC leather and unknown synthetic materials should be avoided.

Choosing the correct leather improves cutting quality, reduces processing issues, and helps create durable, professional finished products.

Frequently Asked Questions

What type of leather is best for laser engraving?

Vegetable-tanned leather and natural genuine leather are commonly preferred because they produce strong engraving contrast and a natural appearance.

Can PU leather be laser cut?

Some PU leather products can be laser processed, but compatibility depends on the coating composition. Always confirm the material specifications before processing.

Why should PVC leather not be laser cut?

PVC may release corrosive hydrogen chloride gas when exposed to laser energy, which can damage equipment and create safety risks.

What thickness of leather is suitable for laser cutting?

Thin to medium leather (approximately 0.5–3 mm) is commonly used for laser products. Thicker leather may require higher-power CO₂ lasers and optimized settings.

Why does leather smell during laser cutting?

Leather contains organic fibers, dyes, oils, and tanning compounds that decompose during laser processing. Proper exhaust ventilation is required to remove smoke and odors.
